sections.h2: Who sends and collects property tax bills in Franklin County, Missouri?
sections.html:
The county collector of revenue bills and collects, and the assessor values the land. Doug Trentmann is the Franklin County Collector, in Room 103 at 400 E Locust in Union, phone 636-583-6353. His office handles current and delinquent taxes for the county and 64 other taxing entities, and also levee, railroad and utility taxes, plus merchant and manufacturer licenses.

The county website lists four ways to pay:

  • Online through the Property Tax Bill Pay page on the county website
  • By phone at 877-690-3729 with jurisdiction code 3570
  • In the Collector's office with a check or cash
  • By mailing a check using the address on the bill

The county notes that a nominal convenience fee is charged for these services.

The assessor does not figure taxes, set rates or print bills. Franklin County's own assessor page says each taxing jurisdiction sets its own levy, so questions about the rate go to those bodies and their annual budget meetings.

sections.h2: What kind of county is Franklin County for a home seller?
sections.html:
Franklin County is a large exurban county on the south side of the Missouri River, part of the St. Louis metro area, with Union as the county seat. It was organized in 1818 and named for Benjamin Franklin. German families arrived in numbers starting in 1833, steamboats once carried freight on the river, and the railroads later made the county a transport center. Wineries around New Haven and Berger sit inside the Hermann American Viticultural Area.

The county covers 923 square miles of land, which makes it the fourth-largest in Missouri by land area. Incorporated places are Berger, Gerald, New Haven, Pacific, St. Clair, Sullivan, Union and Washington. Gray Summit, Lake St. Clair, Stanton and Villa Ridge are census-designated places. A seller in a city pays a city bill too, so a Washington or Pacific address means two sets of statements.

The Census QuickFacts table shows what the housing stock looks like:

  • 108,090 people in the July 2025 estimate, up 3.3 percent from April 2020
  • 48,091 housing units, and 76.5 percent of occupied homes lived in by owners
  • $227,600 typical value for a home lived in by its owner (2020 to 2024 median)
  • $73,165 median household income and a mean commute of 28.3 minutes
  • 794 building permits in 2025

sections.h2: How big is the Franklin County assessment roll?
sections.html:
The Franklin County assessor tracks more than 73,000 parcels with over $1.511 billion in assessed value, the thirteenth highest among Missouri's 114 counties and St. Louis City. Roughly 50,000 parcels are classed residential, 24,000 agricultural and 3,400 commercial. The office says it reassesses all real estate every two years and mails more than 20,000 value-increase notices a year.

Statute fixes the percentages. Under RSMo 137.115, residential property is assessed at 19 percent of true value, agricultural at 12 percent and commercial at 32 percent, with new values set as of January 1 of odd-numbered years. A parcel the assessor wants to raise by more than 15 percent, other than for new building, needs a physical inspection first, and the owner can ask for the inside to be viewed.

The assessor also fields requests from title companies and mortgage lenders, and the county's property search site lets an owner pull up the parcel record before calling. Check the acreage, square footage and bedroom count on the record, since errors there change the value.

sections.h2: What are the key dates on the Franklin County property tax calendar?
sections.html:
The county assessor publishes a yearly calendar that a seller can use to see where a house stands in the cycle. The table lists those dates as the county gives them.

Franklin County assessment and billing calendar, per the assessor
DateWhat happens
January 1Valuation date for all real and personal property
March 1Personal property list due, with penalties if late
June 30Real estate and personal property rolls go to the County Clerk
Second Monday in JulyLast day to file a Board of Equalization appeal
September 30State Tax Commission appeal date, or 30 days after the Board letter if later
October 1Tax rates set and certified to the County Clerk
November and DecemberCollector prepares and sends bills
December 31Current taxes must be paid before they become delinquent

Source: Franklin County Assessor page. Utilities and railroads report to the assessor by April 1, and the clerk certifies those values by April 20.

sections.h2: How do I challenge a Franklin County valuation?
sections.html:
The first call is to the assessor, who holds many informal hearings each year, most of them in a reassessment year. The office says it works to settle owner concerns so fewer reach the Board of Equalization. Ask for the comparison sales the value rests on and compare them with houses near yours.

If that fails, file with the Board of Equalization by the second Monday in July. The Board decides appeals in a summary way and, under RSMo 138.060, no one presumes the assessor is right. Where a value rose at least 15 percent from the last assessment for reasons other than new construction, the assessor has to prove the value does not exceed market value.

If the Board leaves the value in place, RSMo 138.430 gives 30 days after its final action to go to the State Tax Commission. The county's lawyer defends the assessor there. A claim that a property should be exempt rather than reduced goes to the circuit court within 30 days of the Board decision. Missouri's Commission also says an LLC, trust, estate or corporation must use an attorney to file.

sections.h2: Can seniors or disabled owners in Franklin County get property tax relief?
sections.html:
Missouri does not exempt the property of seniors or disabled owners, according to the Franklin County assessor. It points instead to the Missouri Property Tax Credit, which gives income-limited seniors and disabled residents a refund or income tax credit based on property tax or rent paid. Details are at the state Department of Revenue site, and Aging Ahead answers questions at 636-629-3143.

The assessor adds that the Homestead Preservation Act credit needs a legislative appropriation and is not funded at this time.

sections.h2: What happens if Franklin County taxes go unpaid past December 31?
sections.html:
The county says taxes turn delinquent after December 31 and penalties are applied. Under RSMo 139.100, the collector adds the penalty after January 1, and RSMo 140.100 sets it at 18 percent of the year's delinquency, with a 2 percent monthly cap if the land is redeemed before sale. A mailed payment counts on its postmark date.

A taxpayer who disputes the value can pay the full bill before the delinquency date and file a written protest with the collector. The protest must come with a lawsuit against the collector within 90 days under RSMo 139.031. Tax paid by mistake can be credited or refunded on written request filed within three years.

Delinquent land is offered at the sale on the fourth Monday in August under RSMo 140.150, and the owner may pay everything owed at any time before that. The collector mails a first class notice, and a certified one when the assessed value is above $1,000. Ask the Franklin County Collector for the sale date and the amount to redeem.

sections.h2: How do I handle property tax when I sell a Franklin County house?
sections.html:
Pull the parcel from the pay site and print the current bill, then ask the Collector at 636-583-6353 whether any earlier year is open. The title company will need the parcel ID and the figure, and the sales contract decides how the current year is split between buyer and seller.

If the house is inherited, behind on taxes or has tenants or repairs outstanding, a cash buyer can take the house in its current condition, with the tax payoff taken from the price at closing. Franklin County deeds are filed at the Recorder of Deeds, and the county website has a Record My Deeds link on its home page.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Franklin County property tax?
faqs.a: At the Collector's office, Room 103, 400 E Locust in Union, or online, by phone at 877-690-3729 with code 3570, or by mail. The county says a nominal convenience fee applies to these services.

faqs.q: When is the Franklin County tax deadline?
faqs.a: December 31. The assessor's calendar says current taxes must be paid by that date, and after it they are delinquent and penalties are applied.

faqs.q: What is the route for contesting a Franklin County assessment?
faqs.a: File with the Board of Equalization by the second Monday in July. After the Board rules, you have until September 30 or 30 days after its letter, whichever is later, to go to the State Tax Commission.

faqs.q: How often does Franklin County reassess homes?
faqs.a: Every two years. The assessor reassesses all real estate on a two-year cycle, and Missouri law sets new values as of January 1 of odd-numbered years, with new construction valued each year.

faqs.q: Is there property tax relief for Franklin County seniors?
faqs.a: There is a state refund and credit. The Missouri Property Tax Credit helps seniors and disabled residents with limited income. The county assessor notes the Homestead Preservation Act credit is not funded now.
